claims.text: Controlled dealloying of a pre-alloyed noble-metal-rich HEA precursor will yield a three-dimensional nanoframework.
The resulting nanoframework will have interconnected porosity.
Formation of the porous nanoframework will enhance catalytic performance.
The proposed precursor is a bulk HEA containing noble metals and less-noble, more-leachable components.
The precursor components are in near-equiatomic proportions.
Chemical or electrochemical dealloying can selectively remove the more active, less-noble components.
Controlled solution chemistry, potential, and temperature can permit selective etching without structural collapse.
Selective etching creates a bicontinuous porous nanostructure.
During dealloying, the remaining noble-metal atoms reorganize into a three-dimensional framework.
Selective dissolution of less-noble elements induces surface diffusion and atomic rearrangement.
Surface diffusion and atomic rearrangement lead to self-assembly of a porous network.
The dealloyed porous network retains the catalytic versatility of the noble-metal components.
The porous network increases active surface area.
The resulting three-dimensional nanoframework will be robust and have a large surface area and intricate pore connectivity.
Greater exposure of active sites will improve catalytic efficiency.
The untreated HEA precursor has a homogeneous atomic distribution and lacks a high-surface-area nanostructure.
Overly aggressive or poorly controlled dealloying may cause structural collapse or prevent framework formation.
Interactions among multiple elements may produce unpredictable local atomic ordering.
